reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Presents with sore throat, painful swallowing, fever, malaise and tender enlarged jugulodigastric lymph nodes
The follicular (spotted) form shows yellowish exudate at the tonsillar crypt openings, while the membranous form has a coalescent whitish membrane
Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus is the most important bacterial cause because of its non-suppurative sequelae
Viral causes are common; features such as prominent cough, coryza and conjunctivitis point away from streptococcal infection
Consider infectious mononucleosis when there is marked tonsillar enlargement, membrane formation, generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly
Management principles include adequate hydration, analgesia and antibiotics when streptococcal infection is likely, avoiding aminopenicillins if glandular fever is suspected because of the rash
Non-suppurative complications of streptococcal infection include rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis, which justify appropriate antibiotic treatment
Recurrent tonsillitis meeting frequency criteria, or complications such as abscess, may warrant tonsillectomy
reference.pathophysiology: Acute tonsillitis is acute inflammation of the palatine tonsils, usually from viral or bacterial infection of the tonsillar crypts and parenchyma. Pathogens invade the crypt epithelium, provoking an inflammatory response with hyperaemia, oedema and crypt exudate. Streptococcal infection can trigger immune-mediated sequelae elsewhere in the body. Local spread of infection beyond the tonsillar capsule can produce peritonsillar or deep neck space abscesses, and marked tonsillar and adenoid enlargement may compromise the airway.
additionalDifferentials: Agranulocytosis or leukaemic infiltration presenting with sore throat
additionalInvestigations: Throat examination to assess tonsillar size, exudate and membrane
Throat swab or rapid antigen test for group A streptococcus where indicated
Full blood count and monospot or heterophile antibody test when mononucleosis is suspected
Assessment for splenomegaly and generalised lymphadenopathy
Blood glucose and further workup if recurrent or atypical infection suggests immunosuppression
redFlags: Trismus, drooling, muffled voice or unilateral swelling suggesting peritonsillar or deep neck abscess
Stridor or respiratory difficulty from airway obstruction
A grey adherent membrane bleeding on removal, raising concern for diphtheria
Persistent unilateral tonsillar enlargement or ulceration suggesting malignancy
reference.prognosis: Most episodes are self-limiting or resolve promptly with treatment; complications such as abscess formation and, in streptococcal disease, rheumatic and renal sequelae are largely preventable with appropriate management.
pitfalls: Prescribing ampicillin-type antibiotics in undiagnosed glandular fever and precipitating a rash
Missing a developing peritonsillar abscess in a patient with worsening unilateral symptoms
Treating all sore throats as bacterial when many are viral
Overlooking a haematological cause in unusually severe or persistent cases
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Prescribe phenoxymethylpenicillin when streptococcal infection is likely or confirmed, using a macrolide if penicillin-allergic and avoiding aminopenicillins where glandular fever is suspected because of the rash
Provide supportive care with adequate hydration and analgesia and antipyresis using paracetamol or an NSAID
Use a clinical scoring tool with rapid antigen testing or throat swab to target antibiotics and avoid unnecessary prescribing in viral disease
Drain a peritonsillar abscess and treat deep neck space infection, remaining vigilant for airway compromise from marked tonsillar enlargement
Manage suspected infectious mononucleosis supportively and advise temporary avoidance of contact sport where there is splenomegaly
Refer for consideration of tonsillectomy in recurrent or complicated disease
Escalate urgently for airway obstruction, inability to swallow fluids or signs of deep neck space spread
